beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Optimizing GPU Usage on Explorer. How to confirm that a job really used the GPU, measure what it uses, and fix the few problems that waste most GPU time.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. A GPU job that finishes without an error has not necessarily used the GPU. Code that cannot find a card quietly runs on the CPU, and code that finds one may keep it waiting for data. This lecture is a set of measuring tools for Explorer, and a short list of fixes. Measure first. Change second.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. GPU utilization: the share of the last second in which the card ran any work at all. V RAM: the card's own memory, where your model and your batch live. DataLoader: the part of PyTorch that reads, batches and hands data to the card. Profiler: a tool that tells you where the time went. B F sixteen: a sixteen-bit number format that keeps the range of thirty-two-bit floats. And D D P: distributed data parallel, one model copy per card.

beats.act: I · Do You Have The GPU?
beats.narration_text: Never trust the allocation. This verify script checks five things: CUDA available, the cards and their memory, the visible-devices variable, NVIDIA S M I, and a tensor round trip. Available means PyTorch sees a card. The round trip proves it can use one.

beats.narration_text: Slurm sets CUDA visible devices to your cards' numbers: zero is one card, zero comma one is two. Leave it alone unless you want a subset. It can be unset in an interactive session, so it is never proof either way. The round trip is.

beats.narration_text: Now watch it. NVIDIA S M I has two numbers that matter. GPU utilization: the share of the last second in which a kernel was running. In this example, eighty-seven percent, healthy; below fifty means something is wrong. And memory: here, about a fifth of the card.

A small tag 'example' on each. Terracotta only at the mark.

beats.narration_text: To see it live, a person opens a second terminal on the compute node and runs watch. N V I top is a richer view, per process, so you can confirm that your own Python is using the card. A coding agent should not run watch. It never exits.

beats.narration_text: Read them as two axes. High memory with low utilization: loaded, but nothing is feeding it. Low and low: the card sits empty. High utilization with low memory: healthy, raise the batch. High and high: good. Fifteen percent utilization, seventy-five memory? Data starvation.

shot.visual_intent: A drawn 2x2 grid: utilization across (low to high), memory up (low to high). Four cells with short tags: top-left 'loaded, not fed', bottom-left 'empty card', bottom-right 'raise the batch', top-right 'good'. The cells land on the spoken order. Then a terracotta dot drops into the top-left cell at (15, 75) with the mono tag '15% / 75%' and the words 'data starvation'.

beats.narration_text: Use one set of bands. Under fifty percent is a problem. Under sixty, suspect the data pipeline. Sixty to seventy is amber, seventy acceptable, eighty to a hundred the target. For memory, sixty to ninety percent is healthy; under forty means room for a bigger batch.

Bottom 'memory' 0 to 100: under 40 'room to raise batch', 60-90 'healthy'. Segments grow left to right on the spoken numbers.

beats.narration_text: Explorer also watches for idle cards. A bot called Idle Bot emails you after about fif teen minutes of under-use, and the job is cancelled after about an hour. We found no published percentage for under-use. A stalled job holds its card and your queue place while doing nothing.

beats.narration_text: A profiler tells you where the time went. Four layers, lightest first. Live tools: NVIDIA S M I and N V I top. The framework profiler. Nsight Systems for a timeline. And Nsight Compute for one kernel. Stop as soon as you know. Most problems show by layer two.

beats.narration_text: Profile in a short interactive session, not through the batch queue. Get a session on G P U short, activate your environment, run fifty steps, change one thing, repeat. If it runs in under thirty minutes, skip the batch queue.

beats.narration_text: On the timeline, an empty GPU row with short bursts means data arrives late. File reads filling the gaps mean you are reading a network filesystem during training. Copies scattered through each step mean data moves inside the loop. Pin the memory.

beats.narration_text: The most common bottleneck is not the model. A fast cook waits for slow deliveries. Say the card computes a batch in twenty-five milliseconds and the loader needs sixty. The card idles thirty-five of every sixty. No model change fixes that.

beats.narration_text: The fix usually lives in four DataLoader settings. Workers: CPU processes that load in parallel. Pin memory: page-locked RAM for faster copies. Persistent workers: do not restart them every epoch. Pre fetch factor: batches each worker prepares ahead.

props.title: IV · The four settings  ·  as written
lines: num_workers=8,            # ← CPU worker processes for parallel loading
pin_memory=True,          # ← allocate in page-locked RAM for fast GPU transfer
persistent_workers=True,  # ← keep workers alive between epochs
prefetch_factor=4,        # ← batches each worker pre-loads ahead of time

beats.motion_claim: The text, exactly as written or recorded, prints line by line as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: Starting values. Workers: CPUs per task, minus one, never zero. Pin memory: always on in a GPU job. Persistent workers: on whenever workers is above zero. Pre fetch: two, raise it if still slow. So ask for CPUs per task equal to workers plus one, and at least four.

Beneath, a drawn equation of blocks: [--cpus-per-task] = [num_workers] + [1 for the main process], with 'at least 4' tag. beats.narration_text: And never feed the card one item at a time. Every call has a fixed cost: launch, transfer set-up, synchronization. Ten thousand single-sample calls pay it ten thousand times. One batched call pays it once.

beats.narration_text: Where the data lives matters. On Explorer, home, scratch and projects are all network filesystems. Keep data in scratch or a projects folder, packed into a few large files, never millions of small ones, and never in home. Scratch is purged, so keep your original elsewhere.

beats.narration_text: Research Computing's material illustrates the direction. With no workers: about eighteen percent utilization, four hundred twenty images a second. Eight workers and pinned memory: fifty-five percent, thirteen hundred. Add pre fetching: eighty-two percent, nineteen fifty. No script produces these. Use them for direction, not as a promise.

beats.narration_text: Batch size is the simplest lever. Doubling it roughly doubles throughput, until the card is saturated, if the memory is there. If memory sits near twenty percent and nothing fails, double the batch and measure again. Stop short of the largest size that fits, because the optimizer needs memory too.
